All of this interest in the great American pastime
was not a mushroom growth in the head of George
Halas. Ever since 1914-18 when he was playing right
end for Bob Zuppke at Illinois, George has been bitten
He even carried it into the war with him when he
packed up a sailor's dufflebag and left for the Great
As a member of the Great Lakes squad he
played his first game in Southern California, meeting
the Mare Island Marines at old Tournament Park-
the original Rose Bowl in Pasadena.
Only once in his meteoric career in the football
world did George "get out of character." He took a
fling at baseball in 1920, joining the New York
Yankees as an outfielder. However, his diamond dust-
ing carcer ended as abruptly as it opened when he
joined the huge Staley Manufacturing Company at
Decatur, Ill., after the '20 baseball season was fin-
ished. Halas stepped into the Athletic Director's
chair of the big starch works, taking over coaching
and direction of football, baseball, and basketball in
the big commercial circuits then in full swing
The following year Mr. Big of the Big Bears
joined with "Dutch" Sternaman in moving the
Staley's football squad to Chicago where the now
famous Chicago Bears came into being. The first
squad included a number of Halas' former team
mates on the Great Lakes squad as well as some ex-
cellent Staley's material and what gridiron talent was
left lying around after the other nineteen pro clubs
in that section got through picking over the list.
George and Sternaman coached and played until
1928 when Halas dropped out to the sidelines to get
a breath of air and help open the doors of his other
business enterprises. At the opening of the 1929 sea-
son, Ralph Jones was engaged to coach the Bears, and
for the next three seasons he kept the Chicago pro
club hustling, winning a National League champion-
Sternaman who left the squad in 1931 also left a
big vacancy in the coaching department which Halas
filled at the opening of the 1933 season when he again
took over the reins as Mr. Big.
Since the "Revolution" in the National League in
1933 when the strongest clubs were divided into an
Eastern and Western Division, the Bears have won
five sectional titles and two world's championships.
George Halas' directing philosophy is as simple as
his famous "T" formation is intricate. "Make more
touchdowns than your opponents." With that as a
rule of thumb George started out to build up the
hardest punching, most mystifying offense he could
came out with the "Model T" that is the talk of the

Perry Schwartz of Brooklyn gets a showing at end.
